name: Objectivity illusion
statement: Partisans trace their own side's political views to facts and careful thought, and the other side's to misinformation, propaganda and self-interest.
meaning: This is naive realism's third conviction given a name and a number. Ross and Ward's account says that a person takes his own view to be a direct reading of reality, expects reasonable others to share it, and explains dissent by something wrong with the dissenter. Schwalbe, Cohen and Ross took that last step and made it a scale. Participants rate how far supporters of each candidate were influenced by three normative considerations, such as knowledge of facts and history, and by four biases, such as misinformation and propaganda. The illusion is the mean normative rating minus the mean biased rating, for allies minus adversaries. Two things separate the measured construct from the framework it comes from. It is about groups rather than one person against another, and it is scored on why people believe what they do rather than on what they are like. The authors are careful about what 'illusion' claims. They write that they use the term not because the assessments are necessarily wrong, or even equally wrong, but because beliefs are never an unmediated reflection of reality.

origin.who: Michael C. Schwalbe, Geoffrey L. Cohen and Lee D. Ross
origin.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
origin.note: The paper that fixes the label, in the sentence 'We use the term "objectivity illusion" to describe this tendency'. It names naive realism as its starting point and cites Ross and Ward's chapters for that. The phrase is older than the paper: Pronin, Gilovich and Ross's 2004 reference list carries a 1999 dissertation abstract by David A. Armor titled 'The illusion of objectivity: A bias in the perception of freedom from bias', which was not obtained for this entry.

evidence: Study 1 ran on Amazon Mechanical Turk in three stages around the 2016 presidential debates, with 870 people at stage 1, 696 the next day and 509 twenty-four days later. Supporters put their allies at +1.24 on the normative-minus-biased composite, SD = 1.94, and their adversaries at -3.00, SD = 1.89, t(744) = 37.72, P < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.38. The gap tracked partisanship, r = 0.50, running from d = 0.99 among leaners to d = 1.55 among strong supporters and d = 2.08 among very strong ones. It also held for every one of the seven influences taken separately. Undecided voters rated both camps as driven more by bias than by reason, Trump supporters at M = -1.93 and Clinton supporters at M = -1.52, t(124) = -11.69 and t(124) = -9.14, both P < 0.001. Stage 1 and stage 3 scores correlated at r = 0.82. The predictive results are what the paper was written for. Baseline illusion predicted claiming that one's own candidate won the debates, b = 0.17, 95% CI (0.13, 0.20), t(446) = 9.76, P < 0.001, r = 0.42, with 64% of low scorers and 91% of high scorers saying so. It predicted the strengthening of candidate support over the 24 days, b = 0.05, 95% CI (0.02, 0.07), t(446) = 3.29, P = 0.001, r = 0.15. High scorers had a 1.1% chance of switching allegiance or going undecided against 15.4% for low scorers, and a 15.9% chance of picking a free book favouring the opposing candidate against 40.2%. Both relationships survived controls for initial strength of support and for how badly participants rated the other side's personal traits. Study 2, two days before the election, gave 1,715 participants a fictitious blog post by 'Robert Miles' backing one candidate. Ratings of the author ran +2.66 when he backed the participant's candidate and -1.57 when he backed the other, t(1513) = 38.69, P < 0.001, d = 1.98, while undecided voters rated the two versions alike, t(190) = 0.92, P = 0.36, d = 0.13. Between 13.4% and 17.5% of each side called average supporters of the other candidate very or extremely evil. The attribution does not need politics to appear. Cheek, Blackman and Pronin ran seven experiments on judgements of paintings. In their first, 70 undergraduates, cut from 90 after 16 suspected the deception and 4 were dropped for procedural error, rated a stranger who had picked different paintings as less guided by the works' true quality, t(68) = 4.47, P < 0.001, d = 1.07, and more swayed by social influence, t(68) = -2.51, P = 0.015, d = -0.60.

replication.headline: A preregistered census-matched sample of 1,808 Americans reproduced the measure's headline prediction four years later, though two of its authors also wrote the original.
replication.detail: Schwalbe, Joseff, Woolley and Cohen surveyed 1,808 US adults on Lucid in early 2020, quota-matched to the census across gender, age, race, ethnicity, income, education and region. The sample was split before any analysis into a discovery half of 632 and a hold-out validation half of 1,176, each with its own preregistration filed after collection and before analysis. The article's own abstract gives those halves as 630 and 1,100. They used a shortened form of the 2016 scale, two normative items and two biased ones. In the validation sample, objectivity illusion predicted the tendency to judge headlines by whether they flattered one's politics rather than by whether they were true, beta = 0.42, 95% CI [0.36, 0.48], t(859) = 13.62, p < .001, and it came out as one of the two strongest predictors of that bias among every measure in the study. The illusion itself has independent support that predates the label. Kenworthy and Miller's three studies, from a different laboratory, found that people rate their own attitudes as the most rationally and the least externally and emotionally based, out-group attitudes as the reverse, and in-group attitudes in between. No direct replication of either 2016 study was located. The search covered Crossref, PubMed, Semantic Scholar's list of 26 papers citing the 2020 article, and the open web.

study.cite: Schwalbe, M. C., Joseff, K., Woolley, S., & Cohen, G. L. (2024). When politics trumps truth: Political concordance versus veracity as a determinant of believing, sharing, and recalling the news. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 153(10), 2524-2551.

limits: The 2016 evidence is correlational, and the paper says so before its readers can. Its authors also flag the confound that costs the measure most: ratings of influences and ratings of personal traits correlated above r = 0.75, so both may reflect one halo, in which supporters endorse any compliment to their own side and any insult to the other. The defence offered is that the influence measure kept predicting debate perception, closed-mindedness and polarisation after the trait measure was controlled for, while the trait measure did not. Both 2016 studies ran on Mechanical Turk, which the authors call a convenience sample and describe as more homogeneous than the United States. Study 1 lost 42% of its stage 1 participants by stage 3. Study 1 also contained a framing manipulation whose results are not in the paper; the analyses are collapsed across its two conditions, with the effects promised to a later article. Everything here comes from one election in one country, and the scale asks about named candidates rather than about issues. The 2020 follow-up widens the sampling frame but not the setting, since its headlines were all about Donald Trump.
misreadings: The first misreading is that this is a separate discovery. It is the third tenet of naive realism, measured at group level, from the research group that built the framework, and the atlas already carries naive realism, the bias blind spot and the illusion of asymmetric insight from the same programme. What is new in 2020 is longitudinal prediction, not the phenomenon. A reader wanting the underlying account should read the naive realism entry rather than treating these as four findings. The second is that calling it an illusion says both sides are equally mistaken about the facts. Schwalbe and colleagues reject that reading in the discussion, writing that in many disagreements one party may hold views better supported by facts and argument than the other. The illusion they name is the conviction that one's own view alone is free of any lens. The third is that the two camps behaved identically. The composites were largely symmetric, and the items were not. Trump supporters marked the patriotism gap hardest, d = 1.43, where Clinton supporters marked it least, d = 0.25; Clinton supporters marked compassion at d = 1.44 against 0.44. Among very strong supporters the overall gap was wider on the Trump side, Mdiff = +6.43 against +5.57, t(161) = 2.38, P = 0.019, d = 0.31, and the 2020 study again found a stronger illusion among Trump supporters than among his opponents. The fourth is that the illusion has been shown to cause polarisation. The path and mediation models in the paper are fitted to observational data, and the authors write that the correlational nature of the data precludes causal claims. The one experimental handle in this literature is on the input rather than the outcome: Cheek and colleagues manipulated whether a stranger agreed, and disagreement alone was enough to make his judgement look biased.
